description: Hi! We are Luciana and Sebastián, two Ecuadorians studying Business Informatics and Biotechnology in Germany. With backgrounds in technology and life sciences, we are passionate about exploring data and turning it into practical tools that improve health outcomes and make complex processes more accessible and efficient.
summary:
BIORBIT is an offline-first health monitoring software that gives astronauts their full health status in seconds. After a biometric sign-in, a clickable body model, live vitals, and a traffic-light system (green, yellow, red) show the state of numerous body systems, and every alert is explained in plain language with a personalised recommendation. Moreover, instead of only counting radiation dose, BIORBIT tracks early DNA changes in the blood and shows both side by side. Our software also offers a mental health and women’s health tab and protects sensitive data with role-based privacy. Furthermore, Stellar, our multilingual voice-controlled AI assistant, makes complex medical data intuitive and is available at all times.

BIORBIT turns scattered data into clear, on-board decisions, supporting crew autonomy and safety on long-duration missions.
details:
BIORBIT - Space Health Data Analysis

What it does and how it works

BIORBIT is an offline-first health monitoring app for astronauts. It gives each crew member a clear picture of their health in about three seconds. After a biometric sign-in (fingerprint, Face ID, voice or PIN), the home screen shows:

  • live vitals compared with the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline;
  • a clickable human body model with 11 hotspots, where tapping an organ shows its status, charts and recommendations;
  • a radiation gauge that tracks career dose against the 600 mSv limit.

A navigation bar on the left is available on every screen, with one icon per section:

  • Crew overview (only for the commander and the flight surgeon): every crew member’s status in expandable cards.
  • Home: live vitals, the body model, Stellar and the radiation gauge.
  • Body systems: ten systems in green, yellow or red; tapping one opens its recommendations.
  • Charts: trends by day, week, mission or career, compared with the personal baseline or the crew average.
  • Radiation & Genomics: dosimeter dose and the six-gene CHIP panel.
  • Recommendations: personalised actions, each with the reason behind it.
  • Medical history: conditions, medication, allergies, vaccinations, past missions and on-board medical kit expiry dates.
  • Reports: auto-generated weekly, monthly and end-of-mission reports for doctors on Earth.
  • Alerts & log: system alerts plus manual entries for symptoms, mood and exercise.
  • Women’s health: cycle tracking or suppression, symptoms, and a switch to share with the flight surgeon.
  • Mental wellbeing: a 30-second daily check-in with a mood trend.

The top bar adds a red emergency button with guides for the five most likely emergencies, plus help, full screen, the user’s profile, a menu and an Earth-sync indicator that shows when data was last sent to Earth.

In the body systems tab, ten body systems are classified as green (OK), yellow (watch) or red (critical), always shown with colour plus an icon, and every alert explains in plain language what happened and why.

BIORBIT also links radiation exposure to its biological effect. In the Radiation & Genomics tab, a personal dosimeter adds up daily dose (career dose = previous missions + daily dose this mission) and projects it to the end of the mission. A genomic module monitors six genes linked to clonal haematopoiesis (CHIP): DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, TP53, PPM1D and JAK2. Blood would be sequenced on board, for example with a portable nanopore sequencer, and compared with the pre-flight genome. The app calculates the variant allele frequency (VAF = mutant alleles ÷ total alleles × 100) and estimates the share of mutated cells (≈ 2 × VAF). It then applies traffic-light thresholds inspired by the Clonal Haematopoiesis Risk Score.

Other important features are:

  • Stellar, a multilingual AI health assistant with voice control, available on every screen.
  • Trend charts by day, week, mission or career, including comparison with the crew average.
  • Personalised recommendations, each with the reason behind it.
  • Medical history, including expiry tracking for the on-board medical kit.
  • Auto-generated reports for doctors on Earth.
  • Symptom and mood log, plus quick guides for the five most likely emergencies.
  • Private, opt-in sections for women’s health and mental wellbeing.

Benefits and intended impact

On a Mars mission, the one-way signal delay to Earth can reach about 22 minutes, so crews cannot depend on real-time help from the ground. BIORBIT works offline and syncs with Earth when a link is available, and turns scattered data into clear, actionable information on board. The intended impact is earlier detection of problems such as bone loss, radiation-related DNA changes, sleep loss and fluid shifts, less manual paperwork, and more autonomy for crews on long missions.

Tools and technologies

  • App: a single-page web prototype built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG charts and animations. It works in any browser and runs at full screen.
  • Data: all astronaut data is simulated, based on value ranges from published literature.
  • Design: the software interface is 100% ours. It was designed using Canva.
  • Testing and media: Playwright for automated testing.
  • AI disclosure: our logo idea is completely our creation; however, the .jpeg file was generated by Gemini. Moreover, Claude was used as an AI assistant during research and software development. In the prototype, Stellar’s answers are generated by Claude (Anthropic), with speech-to-text and text-to-speech for voice control. On a real mission, Stellar would run on an on-board model.

What makes it creative

  • The body model makes complex health data intuitive, so you can tap an organ instead of reading tables.
    • The flight surgeon sees her own data first, then every crew member’s full health picture.
    • The commander sees only fitness for duty.
    • Each astronaut sees only their own data.
  • A voice-controlled AI assistant can be used hands-free, even while wearing gloves.

Factors we considered

  • Usability in space: dark mode by default for cabin lighting and sleep cycles, large touch targets for gloves, minimal typing, and colour plus icon so status never depends on color alone.
  • Physiology: facial fluid shift can make face recognition fail, so other login methods are available.
  • Privacy and ethics: genetic and reproductive data are private by default, and alerts describe risk, not diagnosis.
  • Communication delay: the app is offline-first, with a “last synced with Earth” indicator.
  • International crews: the interface is in English, with multilingual support from Stellar.
